title: On API Product
description: Anybody can sit down and, in an afternoon, become up to speed and the mechanics of a RESTful API; these are things like what verb to use where, status codes, and resource creation. A person can use their favorite language and quickly put together something that checks all the  functional boxes to be called an API. But that doesn't make a good API Product. So what does?

title: APIs will be Invisible
description: In preparation for the Nordic APIs Seattle event, the speakers were asked a series of questions regarding the past, present, and future of API design. These aren't trivial questions; as developers and designers of complex systems it is important to revisit where we've been in order to steer where we're going. For posterity, I thought I'd share my responses.

title: The Favela vs the Planned Community
description: API Governance is tricky for a number of reasons. The first is that it is an overloaded term, meaning many things to many people. Another reason is that it is hard to visualize just what it attempts to accomplish. Let's address that.

title: How APIs Drive Business Innovation
description: The number of ways that a company can innovate has increased because the nature of their businesses has changed. Increasingly any business is an information business. If that information is valuable good, then APIs are how those goods get to market.

title: Safe Cultures for Sharing Failures
description: It isn't hard to convince people that sharing stories of their work is a good thing. But how do you create a culture of storytelling? More importantly, how do you create a culture where it is safe to tell those less-than-flattering narratives?

title: Storytelling and the Developer's Need to Communicate
description: We talk with co-workers. We discuss things with bosses. Communication is an essential part of being a software developer. So why do we demean it? And what stories does the API community need to be telling right now?

title: The API Economy and the Amen Break
description: The recent trend in APIs is close public access and narrow developers' ability to play with functionality. If the history of electronic music creation is anything to go by, we may be closing ourselves to long term opportunities.

title: Technical Literacy for All
description: What does technical litercy look like in the age of smart phones where you're unable to open things without voiding the warranty? How do we learn when we can no longer 'view source'? How can we overcome the stigma that computers should only be operated under the supervision of an adult? Where is the time to play with technology?

title: My Daughter's Balloon Stand
description: Before becoming a parent, it is easy to assume that the education is one-direction, from the elders to to their offspring. Having been one for many years, however, I am constantly amazed by the amount they teach me. Recently my five year old illuminated a relationship to risk that I'd rather not think about.

title: Detroit and Hypermedia

title: Cooling on the Connected Car
description: Car manufacturers seem intent in trying to make themselves into the next Apple. They are scrambling to set up their own developer programs, app stores, and evangelism teams. But what if the smartest thing we could do is keep cars dumb?

title: NFL and the IoT
description: The IoT (Internet of Things) will connect billions of devices to an already considerable network of information overload. How can we approach that deluge? More importantly, are there opportunities for playing with large scale data collection before it becomes ubiquitous?

Filled with some of the foremost thought experts in the field, the event was an excellent opportunity to reflect on where we've been, the problems with where we are, and what we need to solve in order to get to where we need to be.

title: On Content

Yet when it comes to web content, we would be wise to emulate that organizational model then the Facebook, Twitter, and Medium content cathedrals of our time.
